 1                  I.     INTRODUCTION AND QUALIFICATIONS

 2   Q1.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

3    A.    My name is Jeffery M. Hughes. My business address is 4900 Stan Roberts Avenue,

4          El Paso, Texas 79934 and 3501 Doniphan Drive, Sunland Park, NM 88063.

5

6    Q2.   HOW ARE YOU EMPLOYED?

10   Q3.   PLEASE        SUMMARIZE       YOUR      EDUCATIONAL          AND      BUSINESS

11         BACKGROUND.

12   A.    I graduated from Albuquerque Technical Vocational Institute with a Certificate

13         degree in Electronics Technology in 1995. Upon graduation I was employed by

14         NovaBus Incorporated in Roswell, New Mexico, as an Electronic Technician in the

15         Maintenance Department. My role was to troubleshoot, maintain, and update

16         automated plant equipment at the company’s bus manufacturing facility.

17                In 2001 I was hired by Rea Magnet Wire in Las Cruces, New Mexico, as an

18         Electronic Technician-Maintenance. In April of 2005 I was promoted to Process

19         Engineering Supervisor responsible for developing and controlling manufacturing

20         processes, internal and external audits, and overall plant performance at the wire

21         manufacturing facility.

 4         site and the development of equipment used to grow and harvest algae for oil

 5         extraction, as well as the site maintenance department.

 7         Supervisor at the Rio Grande Power Station. In March 2020 I was promoted to

 8         Interim Maintenance Superintendent, which became permanent in August 2020. In

 9         this role I was responsible for plant maintenance, budgets, and equipment

10         reliability. In August 2021, I was promoted to Manager - Power Plant of the Rio

11         Grande Power Station while also absorbing the role of Maintenance

12         Superintendent. I was laterally transferred to the Newman Power Station as Plant

13         Manager in December 2021. In January 2023, I accepted responsibility as Plant

14         Manager of Newman and Rio Grande Power Stations for the operation,

15         maintenance, and overall performance and budgets of both stations. I am currently

16         Plant Manager of the Newman Power Station overseeing Operations, Maintenance,

17         Engineering and Outage Management teams.

18

20   A.    I oversee operations at the Newman Power Station, ensuring that the facility

4          Manager. The Rio Grande Station includes the first GE LMS100 gas turbine

 3                           II.       PURPOSE OF TESTIMONY

 4   Q6.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?

 5   A.    The purpose of my testimony is to support the necessary and reasonable costs of

 6         EPE’s local generation needed to provide safe and reliable service to EPE's

 7         customers. First, I provide an overview of EPE's system, including EPE’s service

 8         territory and its generating facilities. Next, I discuss the operational practices and

 9         performance metrics that guide the management of our generation assets including

10         both ongoing operations and recent capital improvements since EPE's last rate case

11         in NMPRC Case No. 20-00104-UT ("2020 Rate Case") through the end of September

12         30, 2025, Base Period, adjusted for local generation capital additions placed in

13         service in October, 2025.

14                My testimony additionally addresses the reasonableness of the operations and

15         maintenance ("O&M") expenses related to EPE's local generation together with the

16         level of reasonable and necessary O&M expenses for EPE’s local generation that

17         should be included in rates.

18                Please note that I discuss both total Company and New Mexico jurisdiction

19         generation fleet capital investment and operating costs.       EPE witness Adrian

20         Hernandez, in his direct testimony, addresses allocations of these costs.

21

 1   Q7.   WHAT DOES EPE MEAN BY LOCAL GENERATION?

 3         generating units. Local generation includes Copper, Montana, Newman, and Rio

 4         Grande Power Station units, all of which are gas-fired units.

 7   Q8.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF THIS SECTION OF YOUR TESTIMONY?

11   Q9.   PLEASE DESCRIBE EPE'S SYSTEM.

12   A.    EPE's service territory covers approximately 10,000 square miles extending from

13         Van Horn, Texas, to El Paso to Las Cruces, New Mexico and then further north to

14         Hatch, New Mexico. To serve its customers, EPE uses various resources, including

15         both local and remote generation. Local generating resources are discussed in more

16         detail later in my testimony, while EPE witness Victor Martinez addresses the

17         remote base-load generation resources at Palo Verde Generating Station ("PVGS")

18         in Phoenix, Arizona, and the renewable resources added since EPE’s last base rate

19         case in 2020. EPE has local generation resources that are interconnected to EPE's

20         local transmission network. To access and deliver this power, EPE utilizes its

13   Q12. ARE ALL OF THE GENERATING FACILITIES INCLUDED IN THE

14        ABOVE TABLE JMH-1 AVAILABLE TO SERVE NEW MEXICO LOAD

15        AND ALLOCATED TO ALL NEW MEXICO CUSTOMERS?

16   A.   Except for Community Solar, Newman Unit 6, and Palo Verde Unit 3, all resources

17        in the above table serve New Mexico customers. Additionally, the costs of the solar

18        facilities at Holloman Air Force Base and New Mexico State University are directly

21   Q13. WHY IS EPE'S LOCAL GENERATION NECESSARY?



                                                8
                                          Amended Filing


                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    JEFFERY M. HUGHES

 1   A.   EPE's local generation is necessary for four primary reasons. First, generation from

 2        EPE's local fleet augments its remote generation to meet customer power needs.

 3        Second, local generation is necessary to better follow load as customer energy

 4        demand changes or as energy output from renewable resources changes. Third,

 5        local generation provides load-serving reliability if transmission constraints or

6         outages affect EPE's ability to import energy from remote generation. Fourth,

 7        EPE's local generating fleet provides voltage support, grid stability, and resiliency

 8        throughout EPE's system.

 9

10             B.    LOCAL UNIT OPERATION AND PERFORMANCE

11   Q14. PLEASE BRIEFLY DESCRIBE THE TYPICAL USAGE OF EPE'S LOCAL

12        GENERATION.

13   A.   Generally, EPE's local generation units are used to follow load and compensate for

14        the variable output of renewable resources, provide grid stability, and serve EPE's

15        load obligations.    For the most part, each of the local units can be used

16        interchangeably to satisfy these functions. EPE's load demands are such that, under

17        normal conditions, the older steam units (Newman Units 1, 2 and 3, and Rio Grande

18        Units 7 and 8) are typically backed down to their minimum loads for the low load

19        hours during off-peak periods and are allowed to be economically dispatched

20        during the higher load periods of the daytime peak periods, particularly during the

21        summer. Rio Grande Unit 9 and the MPS units are designed and are routinely


                                                9
                                          Amended Filing


                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    JEFFERY M. HUGHES

1         cycled to meet varying load demands or to displace less efficient generation. Rio

2         Grande 6 has not been included in EPE’s rates since 2016.

3

4    Q15. HOW      DOES       EPE     MATCH          ITS   LOCAL       UNITS      TO     LOAD

5         REQUIREMENTS TO ENSURE THAT UNITS ARE AVAILABLE TO

6         MEET DEMAND?

7    A.   For daily operations, the Company’s load demand profile requires that Newman

8         Units 1 through 4 and Rio Grande Units 7 and 8 be used primarily as load following

9         units. Rio Grande Unit 8 is also used for voltage and reactive support for the

10        system. Rio Grande Unit 9, and MPS Units 1 through 4 are fast-start units that can

11        be cycled and dispatched to meet load obligations and in response to rapidly

12        changing load conditions. The Copper Power Station is a simple cycle combustion

13        turbine generator that is typically used as a peaking unit. It is subject to start-stop

14        cycles but is also used for load following and to meet spinning reserve

15        requirements. Newman Unit 5, when operating in combined cycle mode, is mostly

16        reduced to minimum load during the mid-morning to early-afternoon hours and is

17        base loaded during peak periods and at night based on typical dispatching needs. It

18        can also return to simple cycle peaking mode if needed.

19

20   Q16. DOES THE OPERATION OF EPE'S LOCAL GENERATION FOR

21        PRIMARILY         LOAD       FOLLOWING           AND      VOLTAGE         SUPPORT


                                                10
                                          Amended Filing


                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    JEFFERY M. HUGHES

 1        PURPOSES AFFECT THE UNIT EFFICIENCY LEVELS?

 2   A.   Yes, especially given the age of these units. Units that are cycled or dispatched to

 3        follow daily load fluctuations experience increased mechanical stress due to

 4        frequent changes in thermal gradients. These thermal cycles accelerate normal

 5        wear and tear experienced by the generating unit, which, in turn, cause losses in

 6        efficiency and availability. Additionally, operating at lower output levels during

7         off-peak hours further diminishes efficiency. It is important to note that most units

 8        in EPE's local fleet--specifically Rio Grande Units 7 and 8 and Newman Units 1

 9        through 4--were originally designed and built to serve as base load units. However,

10        these units are now used to follow load and compensate for the variable output of

11        renewable resources, provide grid stability, and serve EPE’s load obligations that

12        exceed those met through the import of low-cost remote generation. In contrast,

13        Rio Grande Unit 9 and MPS Units 1 through 4 are designed to be ramped up and

14        down as needed and therefore allow EPE to meet customer load expectations and

15        renewable generation fluctuations more efficiently.

16

18        THAT HAVE IMPACTED THE GENERAL OPERATION OF THE LOCAL

19        GENERATION FLEET?

20   A.   Yes. In April of 2023, El Paso Electric officially began participating in CAISO's

21        Energy Imbalance Market ("EIM").          The EIM is allowed to dispatch EPE's

 4        see the direct testimony of EPE witness Martinez for more details regarding EPE's

6

7    Q18. HAS PARTICIPATION IN THE EIM INCREASED O&M COSTS FOR

8         EPE?

 9   A.   Yes. In addition to the costs to launch EPE's participation in the market, EPE's

10        local generation fleet has experienced additional starts, run hours, and an increase

11        in unit capacity factors since joining the EIM, particularly with its simple-cycle

12        combustion turbine fleet. The maintenance on these units is determined by the

13        accumulation of run hours and number of times the unit is started. Increasing either

14        the run hours or number of starts will contribute to more frequent maintenance

15        intervals. This has resulted in additional costs and more frequent forced outages on

16        several units. Please see Figures JMH-1 through JMH-4 below for additional

17        information on the associated impacts from EIM that I just described.

21   Q19. IS THE AGE OF EPE'S LOCAL GENERATING FLEET AN IMPORTANT


                                    14
                                              Amended Filing


                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    JEFFERY M. HUGHES

1         CONSIDERATION WHEN EVALUATING UNIT PERFORMANCE?

2    A.   Yes. In broad terms, EPE's local generation is composed of both very new and very

3         old units. Four of EPE's local units are over 57 years old (Rio Grande Unit 7 and

4         Newman Units 1, 2, and 3). Newman Unit 4 entered service in 1975 and is near

5         the end of its operating life. Power plants of that age become less efficient, have

6         less flexible operating characteristics, and are more costly to operate and maintain.

7         After meeting the must-run conditions, different factors are considered. Cost is

8         typically the primary consideration, followed by the efficiency of the unit (i.e., its

9         heat rate). However, EPE's older units, notwithstanding cost or efficiency, are

10        sometimes dispatched first to provide base load power because they are less

11        adaptable to cycling. Additionally, as more solar resources are added to the grid

12        (both utility scale and rooftop solar), these older units are less able to adjust to

13        fluctuations in solar energy output. Unless reliability must-run conditions exist,

14        unit commitment will be based on the lowest heat rate first, thus having the effect

15        of dispatching older units last.

16

17   Q20. ARE THERE ANY UNIQUE CHALLENGES EPE ENCOUNTERS

18         RUNNING OLDER, LESS EFFICIENT UNITS?

19   A.   Yes, there are challenges. Safety is a core value of El Paso Electric, and aging

20        components, equipment and infrastructure pose an increased safety hazard for

21        employees when working around older units relative to newer units. Failure types


                                                   15
                                         Amended Filing


                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    JEFFERY M. HUGHES

 1        and frequencies increase as components and equipment age. For example, steam

 2        piping walls thin, valves can leak or seize, insulation degrades, and metal fatigue

 3        and creep increase, all of which create potentially hazardous conditions.        In

 4        addition, as components age, the Original Equipment Manufacturers stop

 5        supporting the equipment, making repair and replacement difficult and often

 6        expensive.

 7

 8   Q21. HOW DOES THE COMPANY MONITOR THE PERFORMANCE OF ITS

 9        LOCAL GENERATING UNITS?

10   A.   EPE monitors the performance of its local generating units using two key indicators

11        or measurements: (1) net heat rate and (2) equivalent availability factor ("EAF").

12        Both net heat rate and EAF are industry-accepted measurements of generating unit

13        performance. Net heat rate is used to monitor unit thermal efficiency, while EAF

14        is used to measure unit availability based on the percentage of time within a given

 6        system battery to run low. As a result, the main AC lube oil system experienced a

11        Unit 3 caused subsequent damage to the generator lagging and turbine enclosure.

12        Weld repairs and machining of the rotor journals, refurbishment of all bearings,

13        repair of all steam seals, and replacement of several rows of blades were needed to

14        get the unit back to its normal operating condition.

 2   Q83. THE NINETEENTH PROJECT LISTED IN YOUR LARGE CAPITAL

 4        PREHEATER ROTOR REPLACEMENT PROJECT. WHAT WAS THIS

 5        PROJECT AND WHY WAS IT UNDERTAKEN?

 6   A.   The Newman Unit 3 Air Preheater Rotor Replacement Project was undertaken to

 7        restore the air preheater on the Newman Unit 3 boiler to its designed condition. Air

 8        preheaters are typically installed in boilers on conventional steam power generating

 9        units to improve efficiency of the combustion process. In this case, the preheater

10        rotor tube, which is a hollow shaft, had cracked, causing it to bind and stop. Tube

11        replacement required complete disassembly of the equipment. The preheater was

12        rebuilt and reinstalled as new to include heating elements, seals, bearings, gears,

13        and other miscellaneous parts and components.

19   A.   The Copper Hot Gas Path Inspection Project expanded into a major overhaul of the

20        GE 7EA to resolve critical reliability concerns and ensure sustained full-load

21        operations. The GE 7EA is a large, utility-class industrial gas turbine that serves

 1      as a critical production asset. Because the turbine represents a single-point-of

 2      failure for unit output, degradation of hot gas path and rotating components directly

 3      increases the risk of forced outages, capacity loss, and unplanned capital exposure.

 4      The primary purpose of this project was to restore the unit’s performance and

 5      reliability. All 17 compressor rows were replaced, this also included new inlet

6       guide vanes which were replaced using new blades. The turbine section received

 7      new R1 blades, new R1 vanes, new combustion baskets, cross-flame tubes, and a

 8      new rotor air-cooling pipe.     Remaining combustion and turbine components

 9      underwent comprehensive repairs and recoating to ensure they were returned to

10      optimal operating condition. In addition to these major component replacements,

11      the outage also included several casing leak repairs and other corrective scopes that

12      had previously limited unit performance and reliability. Collectively, these actions

13      were essential to restoring the unit’s output capability, ensuring operational

14      integrity, and supporting dependable service for customers. This project and the

15      overhaul restored OEM compliance, strengthened unit integrity, and mitigated

16      failure risks. This proactive approach improves long-term reliability, supports safe

17      operations, and protects production capacity by minimizing the likelihood of

18      unplanned outages.
